 Features The Nights Before Christmas Review: Tyler Hynes Will Make You Cry About Time
 Erin E. Gross 
 20 hours ago 
 0 
 It’s always funny to watch me watch a Tyler Hynes movie. Not in a bad way! Every movie feels different, but my first remark is always the same: “There’s a cable knit sweater.” I know it will appear somewhere. It’s like a sign that the holidays have officially begun — my own personal first snow. With this one, I didn’t have to wait long. It showed up in the first scene, and I settled into the couch knowing all was right with Countdown to Christmas. 
 And don’t worry – Tyler’s got the candy cane hanging from his mouth (toothpick the rest of the year) appears seven minutes and thirty seconds in. The man is nothing if not consistent, and honestly, there’s something comforting about that. Some actors you trust with a role. Tyler Hynes you trust with a habit and a role. 
 MARTYS WISH
 Tyler plays Marty, a man who asks for more time. Time to read the book, learn the language, learn the craft, and really enjoy it all — and for a while, the movie lets him have it. This is the quietly brilliant thing about the setup: The Nights Before Christmas understands that a time loop isn’t a prison until it’s empty of purpose. Marty learns painting and instruments and languages. He tells the folks at the bar exactly who they are, with the confidence of a man who’s had a hundred rehearsals. He doesn’t mind the loop at all. Why would he? The loop is a gift. How many of us have said, into the cold air of a December, “I just wish I had more time?’
 The movie takes that wish seriously — and then asks what happens when you actually get it.
 What happens is – you meet someone.
 The gift of time is a tricky thing, though. You remember, and no one else does. He finds Chloe in an alley, in tears, insisting it’s “a long story” — but he watched her pick up those ornaments, one by one, like they mattered, and the little smirk on his face? That’s a man already smitten. There’s a whole silent movie in that smirk. It’s the look of someone who has all the time in the world suddenly realizing he wants to spend it on one person.
 CHLOE BELIEVES
 This is where I have to hand it to Laci J Mailey, because what she does in this role is harder than it looks. Chloe learns her new friend is reliving the same day forever, and she doesn’t panic or run. She just asks, “What are you doing with your next tomorrow?” Mailey plays that line with such easy, open warmth that believing this man feels not just plausible but inevitable. She gives Chloe this innocence and, underneath it, this quiet steel — the kind of person who can have the worst day of her life and still stand in an alley caring for broken ornaments. Mailey is the reason the premise feels grounded instead of gimmicky. She doesn’t play the time loop; she plays the person in front of her , and that choice makes every reset land like a small heartbreak.
 THE INVESTMENT
 And Tyler. Tyler Hynes in this movie, you guys. He’s always making us invested in his character, and for some reason Marty is no different. I say some reason because at the beginning of the movie, he’s just kind of meh about things — drifting through a loop of his own making, collecting skills the way some of us collect unread books. It’s meeting Chloe that gives him direction, and I loved that. Sometimes finding the person who gives you hope is exactly what we all need. That’s the transformation Hynes is really playing: not a man learning to escape a time loop, but a man learning to want a tomorrow . And you can see it in the smallest choices — the flicker of nerves, the way Marty suddenly cares how he comes across, the way he studies her like she’s the one new thing in a world he’s already memorized. When Marty knows no one will remember, he’s open and blunt and honey — completely unbothered. But with Chloe? Everything changes. That’s what Hynes does better than almost anyone: the tiny, wordless beats that tell you a man is falling in love before he ever says it.
 When Marty knows no one will remember, he’s open and blunt and honest — completely unbothered by how he comes across. But with Chloe? Everything changes, and you can see it in the smallest choices: the flicker of nerves, the way Marty suddenly cares , the way he studies her like she’s the one new thing in a world he’s already memorized. That’s what Hynes does better than almost anyone — the tiny, wordless beats that tell you a man is falling in love before he ever says it. And when the loop gives us Hynes in glasses and a new grey sweater? A gift to us all. But the moment that undid me was quieter: Marty listing all the things he’s learned, all the people he’s met, and Hynes letting a little loneliness flicker through the bravado Marty showed. Mastery without anyone to share it with is just a very organized kind of alone.
 RESETS ARE A PAIN
 Because Marty is learning about Chloe every time the day resets. He asks about her dream guy — then tries to become that person. And look, who doesn’t love a sharp-dressed man? Drool-worthy, truly. But here’s where the movie got genuinely interesting for me, because this is where it starts asking a real question: is a person built from your own research still a person, or just a mirror? Part of the fun of a relationship is the chaos — the stumbling, the getting it wrong, the mortifying, joyful work of learning someone’s real, imperfect self. Marty becomes too perfect, and that’s a red flag, at least for me. Love that costs you nothing and risks nothing isn’t love; it’s a performance. Give me the imperfections. That’s where the love story actually lives.
 Marty doesn’t mind the loop — until Chloe. Then all he wants is time with her. A simple request, and an enormous one, because there’s no manual for getting out. Watching him try everything and slowly start to fear he’s stuck hurts — but the joy that pours out of him whenever he’s with her? Hynes plays both at once, the sadness and the joy living on the same face, and it wrecked me. That duality is the whole movie in miniature – a man with infinite time discovering that infinite time means nothing without someone to give it to.
 FALLING
 It’s hard to watch him fall in love knowing he has to win her all over again every morning. When he tries to say he loves her, time resets before he can finish. There’s something almost unbearably true about that. Haven’t we all had words we didn’t get to say in time? Marty’s loop just makes the deadline literal. So he decides that until he breaks it, he’ll spend every minute he can with her — because even borrowed days count if you fill them right.
 And having to relive his family’s Christmas Eve dinner sounds like a nightmare, but I think it’s exactly what he needed. Anyone who grew up with holidays split across more than one table knows: family dinners are where we rehearse who we are. His family accepts her, and his mom can see plain as day that they’re in love. The loop keeps giving Marty second chances with strangers all over New York, but it’s the same people at the same table who finally show him what a life actually looks like — messy, repeated, warm.
 I cried when he walked her home, looked at her, and said, “Stay with me. I don’t want to wake up yet.” She kisses him, and it’s like watching two people who genuinely need each other. But because he never gets a second day with her, he decides to stay away. He loves her, and he hates the universe’s cruel joke. That’s the thing about time — the cruelty is never in how much of it we have. It’s in how much of it we spend afraid. 
 THE MOMENTS
 We all underestimate moments. Reliving the times of hurt is something nobody wants — but changing them is the scary, beautiful opportunity. When Marty finally realizes not everything is about him, he knows he has to make a difference. So he drives to Ohio to get her family — because he knows she loves experiences, and there’s nothing better than giving someone the Christmas they actually want, not the one that photographs well. It takes him a few tries to get it right (a detail I adore, because even loop-magic Marty has to practice). The way she lights up when she sees them is everything to him. He takes off before the moment can land, and she comes after him to thank him. He’s invited upstairs, but just seeing her happy is enough. It’s the most Christmas ending imaginable -joy given away on purpose, no receipt required.
 Sometimes we forget that we need people. We need someone to see us. Marty sees her — and he breaks the loop by bringing her family to her. The lesson hides in plain sight: the loop never breaks because Marty finally gets everything right. It breaks because he finally gets outside himself . The magic was never about escaping the day. It was about loving someone inside it.
 TIME 
 I’m no wordsmith, but here’s what I know – we all have to stop taking time for granted. We assume there will be more of it, but time is fleeting and tomorrow is never promised — and that’s exactly why Christmas matters. It’s the one season built entirely around the act of showing up: the same songs, the same recipes, the same people at the same table, over and over, until the repetition itself becomes love. Every Christmas Eve is a loop, if you’re lucky enough to keep getting them. Marty breaking the curse meant everything because he finally understood that. The world is full of people, but what matters is embracing the ones sharing their time and their love with you.
 Give of yourself. Love others. It’s the time of year to do just that.
